doc.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

title: Pay with Basie and films without royalties
summary: Tate says pay was low, films brought flat salaries with no royalties.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: And that is another issue which I’d like you to elaborate on for a moment, and that is part of the structure of these interviews is also talking about how some of our greatest artists, particularly in jazz, don’t get their due or don’t get the respect that is afforded to rap artists or rock artists when what they do sometimes a great deal more artistic and actually costs them more in terms of the time and years they’ve put in in terms of study of their craft. When you started with the Basie band, what kind of money was a musician making at that time?
Not much. The first band we weren’t making anything. And in the latter band in 1939, we —
What were you coming home with, a week, in your pocket?

I’d say in the last band, you mean in the ‘39 band? Well it was better then, but not as ... what it should have been. We made several films and we would kind of get over, because we made “Hit Parade” of ‘43, with Dorothy Dandridge, and “Hellzapoppin” with Olson and Johnson I believe it was. Then we made some money with Ethel Waters, and was Lena Horne in there, I think she, no that was Cab in “Stormy Weather.” But when we made those films and things we made —
So you’d get royalties from that?
No we didn’t get no royalties, we would be paid a flat salary. [inaudible]
That’s right, it should have been, but no. I don’t even think Basie was getting any royalties, but it should have been, and you got paid and that was it.
